epigraph.text: The credit belongs to the man who is actually in the arena . . . who errs, and comes short again and again, because there is no effort without error and shortcoming.
epigraph.cite: Theodore Roosevelt, “Citizenship in a Republic,” Sorbonne, Paris, 23 April 1910
epigraph._source_record: DOC_BANK/Arena/text/tr-citizenship-in-a-republic-1910.json on Sam's desk. Named public-domain edition: African and European Addresses, ed. Lawrence F. Abbott, 1910. Filed BEFORE the words were used, per canon §6. Sam's own fetch carried the common misquotation (“who neither know victory nor defeat”); the edition reads “who know neither victory nor defeat.” Written from memory it would have shipped wrong past every green gate.
epigraph._gendered_noun: “the man who is actually in the arena” is the 1910 text and is never altered. Sam shipped the full credit line deliberately; BK can swap to “There is no effort without error and shortcoming.” with one word. Both options are on the bank record.

intro: That’s where the name comes from. The person who actually steps into the ring — not the one in the stands with an opinion about it. The one down there gets it wrong, over and over, and gets back up. That’s the only way anybody gets good at anything, and it’s how you’re going to get good at this.

So here’s the deal. Nothing in here is graded. Nothing in here counts against you, ever. This is where you get to be wrong cheaply — as many times as you want — so that when it counts, you’ve already made the mistake and you know what it looks like.
Pick your door. I’ll be with you the whole way.

door_enter: Everything behind this door is practice. None of it goes in the gradebook. That's the point — this is where you get it wrong cheaply.
This is your Arena. Same moves we work on in class, no grade attached. Take a swing.
Nothing in here counts against you. Come in, try things, find out what you actually know.
Welcome in. The work behind this door is the work we do in class — just without anybody keeping score.

stations: Each station is one move. Pick the one you want to get better at — you don't have to go in order.
One move per station. Start wherever you want to start.
These are the moves you're graded on in class. In here they're just practice.
units: These rooms follow the units. Go back into one any time — nothing in here closes.
Every unit we finish gets a room. They stay open.
Pick a unit. Everything we've done is still in here.
regents: This lane is the exam itself — the real thing, in pieces small enough to practice.
Everything in here came off a real exam. Small pieces, one at a time.
This is exam practice. Same questions, no pressure attached.

contextualization: Context is the room a document is standing in. Not what it says — what was going on around it.
This one asks where we are, when we are, and what everybody was arguing about. Before you read a word of the document.
Historical context: the situation the document was written into. Set the scene, then read.
sourcing-hipp: Who made this, when, and what did they want from you? That's sourcing.
Every document was made by somebody with a reason. This station is about finding the reason.
Read the source line first — the name, the date, the kind of document. It tells you how to read the rest.
opvl: Origin, purpose, value, limitation. Where it came from, why, what it's good for, and where it runs out.
Every document is useful for something and useless for something else. This station is about naming both.
OPVL: what this document can tell you, and what it can't. Both answers count.
argument-development: A claim that answers the question, in one sentence. That's all a thesis is.
This station is about taking a position. Not describing — deciding, and saying so.
Answer the question in a sentence somebody could disagree with. That's the move.

contextualization: You set the scene before you touched the document. That's exactly the move.
That's context — the time, the place, the argument. Well done.
You gave me the world around it, not a summary of it. That's the hard part, and you did it.
sourcing-hipp: You used the source line, not just the passage. That's the move.
You named who made it and what they wanted. That's sourcing done right.
Good — you read the author's purpose, not only their words.
opvl: You named what it's good for and where it stops. That's the whole move.
That's a real limitation — not 'it's biased,' but what the bias actually costs.
Good. You treated the document as evidence for something specific.
argument-development: That's a claim, not a summary. Somebody could argue with it — that's what makes it a thesis.
You answered the question and took a side. That's the move.
Clear position, one sentence. That's what the essay needs in its first paragraph.

contextualization: That's what the document says. The move asks what was happening around it — same year, same place, same argument everybody was having.
Close. You're inside the document; step outside it. What else was going on then?
Start with the date and the place, then tell me one thing happening at that moment. That's your context.
sourcing-hipp: You named the source. Now say what they wanted from whoever was reading it.
Go back to the line above the passage. Who wrote it, when, and why does that change what it's worth?
That's the content. Sourcing asks about the person behind it — their position, their purpose, their moment.
opvl: 'Biased' isn't a limitation yet. Say what it keeps you from knowing.
You've got origin and purpose. Now: what is this document good for — and what would you not trust it about?
Push one step further. Useful for whom, about what, and what's missing from it?
argument-development: That's true, but nobody would argue with it. Take a position somebody could push back on.
You described what happened. Now tell me what you think about it, in one sentence.
Answer the question directly. Start with 'because' or 'although' and see what comes out.

contextualization: You can set a scene now. That's the opening sentence of every essay this course asks you to write.
That's contextualization — the most-missed point on the short essay, and you just practiced it.
sourcing-hipp: You can size up a document by who made it. That pays on every document question on the exam.
That's sourcing. From here on, read the source line first — every time.
opvl: You can say what a document is worth and where it runs out. That's the difference between using evidence and quoting it.
That's OPVL. It's the move that turns a document into proof.
argument-development: You can put a claim on the page. Everything else in an essay is holding that sentence up.
That's a thesis. Every essay you write this year starts with one.

attempt_again: Good. Go again — you've got more of it than you think.
That's how it works. Second look, fresh eyes.
Round two. Start from the part you were sure about.
Try it again. You're closer than that last one made it look.
idle_nudge: Still with me? Start with the source line — it's doing more work than it looks like.
Take your time. If you're stuck, read it once more and just say what you notice.
No rush. Pick one thing in front of you and start there.
Still there? Say the easy part out loud first. The rest usually follows.
signoff: Good work. Come back to this one whenever.
That's the kind of practice that shows up on the test. See you in class.
Done. That one's in the bank.
